Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire in 380 CE, specifically on February 27, 380, when Eastern Roman Emperor Theodosius I issued the Edict of Thessalonica [d3][d8][d9]. Theodosius I (reigned 379–395 CE) formally made Catholic Christianity the official religion of the empire, closing pagan temples and forbidding pagan worship [d2][d1]. This was the culmination of a longer process: earlier, in 313 CE, Emperor Constantine had issued the Edict of Milan accepting Christianity, beginning the transformation of the church's relationship with the imperial government [d4][d2]. It is also worth noting that Armenia had become the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion even earlier, in 301 CE [d5], while the Roman Empire's formal declaration came under Theodosius I at the end of the 4th century [d7][d8].
